images.caption: Figure 2:Overview. Left: a hairstyle is a set of hair cards. Each card, a polyline of control points with width and thickness, becomes one token holding its root position, root normal, card VAE latent𝐳\mathbf{z}, cross-section type and existence flag. Middle: the set DiT denoises the token set with flow matching, attending across cards and to the condition, a point cloud or an image. Empty slots let the model decide how many cards to generate. Right: the card VAE decodes the tokens into cards, and the chain DiT generates their spring-bone chains.

Figure 3:Network design. Top: the card VAE. The encoder reads the control points of one card with their arc-length fractionsuiu_{i}, plus a learned summary token[CLS], whose output alone gives the mean and log-variance of the 32-d latent𝐳\mathbf{z}. The decoder predicts the number of pointsnnand evaluates the card atnnuniformly spaced arc-length fractions, modulated by𝐳\mathbf{z}(adaLN-Zero). Bottom: both DiTs use the same block design (left), modulated by the timestep and the pooled condition. The set DiT predicts the velocity of 192 card token slots without positional embedding, conditioned on a point cloud or an image. The chain DiT does the same for 48 spring-bone chain slots, conditioned on the card tokens sampled by the set DiT (dashed arrow). Empty slots (dashed boxes) have existence−1-1, filled ones +1.

Figure 4:Point clouds from CHARM’s test set. CHARM and HairDeck output hair cards, colored per card like the artist ground truth; MeshAnything V2, DeepMesh and BPT output meshes. All results are shown on a fixed head at each character’s placement.

Figure 5:Head frame. (a) The dataset frame scales every character to height 1, so heads differ in size and height; the right character’s ears count toward its height and lower its head. (b) In the head frame, all characters share the face widthWWand face topOO.

Figure 6:Single images: two in-the-wild illustrations (top) and an AI-generated photorealistic portrait (bottom). Insets show the outlined regions with mesh edges. TRELLIS.2 and Hunyuan3D-2.1 take the hair region as input, and TRELLIS.2 outputs a flat plate facing the camera for both illustrations. Each card has its own color.
Figure 7:Hairstyles generated by HairDeck from in-the-wild images. Hair colors are taken from the images for display.

Figure 8:Generated spring bones in motion. Left: the generated cards (transparent) with their generated spring-bone chains. Right: a 50° head turn; top row with the chains, bottom row without them. The orange outline marks the hair without spring bones in the same frame.

Figure 9:Interpolation between two test point clouds, inputs A and B: the condition tokens of B are matched to those of A and blended with the weightα\alphaunder each column, and all samples share the initial noise. Hair colors and head placements are blended for display.

Figure 15:Card tokens. A set DiT of the same architecture, trained with each card token ofTab.6, generates two test hairstyles from point clouds; insets magnify the same window in each row. Raw control points and the VAE with index decoding give jagged cards, PCA with 64 coefficients gives straighter cards than the artists’, and our latent gives cards as smooth as theirs. Each card has its own color.
